also: I was so sorry to hear

terms.gloss: I am sorry, it grieves me (what has happened to you)
terms.grammar: with the accusative and infinitive, or quod with the indicative: molestē ferō patrem tuum dēcessisse
evidence: Sen. Ep. 63.1: molestē ferō dēcessisse Flaccum, amīcum tuum
terms.comment: How Seneca begins his letter to a friend who has lost a friend, and Servius Sulpicius his letter to Cicero on the death of Tullia: the plain words for being sorry at someone’s loss. Dēcēdere, “to depart”, is the gentle verb for dying (see “die”). The same phrase means “be annoyed at” elsewhere (see “trouble”), so let the sentence say what you are sorry for.

terms.gloss: how sad; I’m sorry (on hearing bad news)
terms.comment: Chremes’s reply when he hears that a woman he knew has died: the short spoken answer to sad news.

terms.gloss: I am sorry for your sake
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.11.1: nōn tam meā quam tuā causā doleō tē nōn valēre
terms.comment: Cicero to Tiro, of his illness; said to someone in mourning, it is sympathy itself.

phrases.latin: Molestē ferō dēcessisse Flaccum, amīcum tuum
phrases.english: I am sorry that your friend Flaccus has died

phrases.latin: Posteāquam mihi renūntiātum est dē obitū Tulliae, fīliae tuae, sānē quam prō eō ac dēbuī graviter molestēque tulī commūnemque eam calamitātem exīstimāvī
phrases.english: When the news of the death of your daughter Tullia was brought to me, I was, as I ought to be, deeply grieved, and I counted it a misfortune we shared

phrases.latin: Audīvī dē patre tuō. Molestē ferō, et tuā causā doleō.
phrases.english: I heard about your father. I’m so sorry for your loss.

sources: Lewis & Short: molestus · Lewis & Short: doleo · Lewis & Short: decedo
